items.note: Cunningham probed Sanchi, Vidisha and Bharhut, found relics and over 200 short inscriptions at Sanchi, wrote The Bhilsa Topes, and saw Heliodorus's pillar at Vidisha.
The Archaeological Survey of India was formed in 1861, with Cunningham as first Director General.
Udaipur is a region rich in stone quarries; a ground report says illegal quarries run on over 2,500 hectares of forest-department land.
Some believe ground blasts from legal and illegal stone mining pose an existential threat to the temple.
Author describes a network of illegal sand and stone mining involving local party agents, forest department, police and administration.

INTACH's team saw thousand-year-old tanks and stepwells, Nataraja Shiva on a 27-foot rock at Ravan Toll, Pisanhari temple, hill fortification, Bija Mandal, a Jain residence, old doorways, big market and palace ruins; found immediate large-scale conservation needed.
Author says that after well over a century since Garde, archaeology officer of Gwalior's Scindia State, this was the first time anyone took heed of Udaipur at this level.
INTACH drew up a fieldwork plan; four technically skilled members camped in Udaipur until the work was completed.
Local people saw the effort as the start of development that would bring outsiders and help their businesses.
Author and Dr Mishra met the ASI Regional Director, who is based in Bhopal with charge of three states.
A splendid Uma-Maheshwar image went missing; author says centuries-old images lie ownerless in bushes, forests, mounds and fields around Udaipur.
Local farmer-activist Praveen Sharma photographs and relocates images and posts them online; he had placed the missing image four days earlier.
Author imagines a craftsman carving deities for a king, priests singing praises for centuries, and gardeners bringing fresh flowers each morning for Neelkanth (inference).
Theft of the image was reported to the ASI regional director, who asked that an FIR be registered.
The image theft was reported at the DGP's office and then registered in the police station daily register.
Reports of stolen images go from the police station to Interpol; about 250 ancient images recently called back to India; thefts continue.
Behind Bija Mandal the stones show several periods; rear of a Ram temple oldest, old market shops later; all more than five hundred years old.
Small unseen temple on a seven-foot platform in a corner of a vast precinct amid rubble and bushes.
A big fair is held at Udaipur every year on Mahashivratri; thousands come from surrounding districts.
On Mahashivratri a long throng advanced to the temple; four hundred police were deployed for the thousands of devotees.
Narrow temple on a seven-foot platform with a worn Ganesha figure on its door; small like an ascetic's meditation place.
Archaeologist Narayan Vyas assessed the small temple as of the 16th century, after Udayaditya.
Author calls Udayaditya, after whom the city is named, the 12th Paramara king and a kinsman (bandhu) of Bhoj, probably made feudatory here (author's inference).

claim.value: bandhu (kinsman) of Raja Bhoj; 12th Paramara king; inferred feudatory

items.note: Udaipur on the geographic border of the Paramara realm; hill fortification and vast palace precinct suggest Paramara kin lived here to guard the border.
Abundant stone let the Paramaras build temples, palaces, tanks, stepwells and Sanskrit centres; Bhoj's Samarangana Sutradhara cited as testimony.
Temple maintenance was done under Garde's supervision in the time of the Scindia royal house.

Narayan Vyas joined the ASI in 1972 and was posted to Udaipur; houses were built against three sides of the temple; occupants were removed with compensation and four feet of rubble cleared to reveal the foundation.
Two houses in front of the temple were left out and remain occupied; the encroachment was not removed.
Remains of an 80-km wall near Raisen possibly the boundary between the Paramaras and the Kalachuris.
In 1972 Vyas saw the first cleaning of the temple surroundings; after the ASI took the temple under its shelter that was the first big visible work.
State government spent Rs 1.10 crore in five years on four protected monuments (two mosques, Pisanhari temple, 27-foot Nataraja at Ravan Toll); Rs 67 lakh reportedly on one mosque.
One of the two mosques is called 'kachahari' (court) by locals, now a Jama Masjid remembered by Jahangir's name; something written on stone of Jahangir's time must have been found.
Author says this kachahari or Jama Masjid was part of the Paramara palace, in a four-bigha courtyard with four bastions and twenty-foot walls.
ASI staff fail to direct temple visitors to other places in Udaipur such as Ravan Toll and Pisanhari.
Proposal: a weekly heritage walk with printed material, low-budget, supported by Centre, state, district archaeology association or panchayat.
District archaeology association meets at Vidisha once in two or four years; last held one and a half years earlier.
Proposal: make visits compulsory for schools and colleges, with the full documented history told to children.
Minhaj Siraj wrote in Tabaqat-e-Nasiri that the Vidisha temple was 105 gaz high.
Devapaladeva's inscriptions tell that Iltutmish's chieftain posted at Vidisha was struck down; Vidisha again under Paramara dominion.
Author thinks Udaipur's ancestors saved the temple built by Udayaditya, which survived to a large extent among demolished temples.

claim.value: ancestors saved the temple from Tughlaq's plunderers (author's view)

items.note: Author calls Narvarman Udayaditya's son and the 13th Paramara Maharaj, whose Vijay Mandir at Vidisha lasted only a hundred years while his father's work stands.
Images at the temple are disfigured, hands and feet broken, marks of attack clear.
Failed wall attempt at the temple's rear; north and south doors stand with Tughlaq's inscriptions.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's inscription in the temple; author says the temple was not harmed under later rulers.
Closing the western door, a small place of worship was raised; the western door was built from rubble of broken mandapas in the precinct.
Chanderi Gate: possible old temple, loose images and pillars; small later mosque of temple rubble; five to seven samadhis and sati pillars nearby.
INTACH measured Uday Samudra at 980 metres; ghats now descend into wheat fields; shells and a copper coin found in digging.

claim.value: tank built by Udayaditya, 980 m long, now fields

items.note: Dam and reservoir construction was the Paramaras' expertise; reservoirs served caravans and cattle in the dry season.
Besides Uday Samudra, countless stepwells were built in Udaipur.
The government department spent 76 lakh rupees on two mosques while the sati pillars decay.
A reclining image at Uday Samudra is considered a royal dancer called Bedni Mata; local story says she danced on a thread across the reservoir, fell and died; it is her samadhi.

claim.value: royal dancer on a thread over the reservoir; fell; samadhi

items.note: Author notes it is not known since when the story is current or in whose reign she lived.
Narayan Vyas says on viewing the image that it is of a yaksha.
Author imagines the temple's flag-hoisting ceremony on 30 March 1080 (speculative).

off-topic digression on Istanbul excavation and political polemic; nothing citable for any unit

items.note: John Malcolm found Paramara remnants as small principalities; the ruler of Saunti claims descent from the ancient Panwars of Dhar.
refs: John Malcolm, diary translated by Dr Suresh Mishra

items.note: Malcolm says the Panwar Rajputs are considered more honourable than other dynasties in Central India; defeated by Muslims; a chieftain later settled in Dhar as a Maratha king's attendant.
Malcolm saw Paramara descendants living with respect centuries later, aware of their great ancestors.

reject_reason: pilot-judged for C01; nothing for C02–C13 (speculative proposals about descendants)

items.note: Author calls Udaipur a poem on stones; says three years were taken and thousands of artisans displayed their art.
Such vast creations show a prosperous economy; Udayaditya built the temple and the common populace contributed too.
Redemption is not mere polishing of the temple; tourism should spread but the call must touch the soul.
Countless inscriptions are documents engraved on the stones; Pandit Shringavas and Pandit Mahipal speak on entering the temple.
Cleaning of the mounds and excavation of the ruins are necessary.
Cleaning of mounds and excavation of ruins called necessary.
Udaipur's lanes await students who will look into the past.
